fetched_contents.text: Immunity to gastrointestinal nematodes in ruminants: effector cell mechanisms and cytokines Abstract Gastrointestinal nematodes (GINs) of ruminants are prevalent and have major economic impacts worldwide. The insight studies of immune responses triggered against GINs are of great concern to understand interaction between host’s immune system and parasite. T-helper 2 cytokines drive the effector cell mechanisms which include eosinophils and mast cells. The immune responses are controlled by Th2 secreted interleukins (IL); IL3, IL-4, IL-5, IL-9, IL-10 and IL-13. B-Cell immune response is incorporated in defense mechanisms developed against GINs specially immunoglobulins (Ig); IgA, IgE and IgG. The immune resistance of the infected host is presented by failure of larval establishment or hypobiosis, low worm burden and decreased female fecundity. The host–parasite interaction is a complex series that affected by host’s genetic constitution, nutrition, age and physiological status. The GINs have different immune evasion mechanisms to improve their survival within the host. Also, management of the host influences GINs parasitism. Thus, the aim of this review is to highlight the hallmarks of immune responses that endorse GINs parasitism. The insights studies of the triggered immune responses developed against GINs will improve the appropriate protective immune strategy. Keywords: GINs, Cytokines, MMC, Eosinophils, Ruminants, Evasion Introduction Gastrointestinal nematodes of the ruminants’ livestock are highly complex multicellular parasitic organisms that cause gastroenteric verminosis (McRae et al. 2015; Belina et al. 2017). The nematode infections usually elicit serious pathophysiological disorders causing significant economic losses in livestock. They cause severe anemia, loss of appetite and poor growths, consequently lead to losses in meat, milk and wool production and sometimes deaths occur (González et al. 2003; Toscan et al.2017). The life cycle of nematode parasites consists of two phases, pre-parasitic (free-living) and parasitic. The pre-parasitic phase takes place in the environmental surroundings, while the parasitic phase occurs inside the susceptible host. The vast majority of nematode’ life cycles consists of egg, five larval (L) stages; L1, L2, L3, L4 and L5 and adult stage. The third larval stage is the infective stage that penetrates the intestinal mucosa and matures to L4 then L5 (immature adult stage) and finally to adult stage. The successful infection is contributed to health status and immunity of the infected hosts (Angulo-Cubillán et al. 2007; Kandil et al. 2017). Both the innate and adaptive immune responses are the classical pathways to kill and/or expel the parasitic nematode or to exacerbate a disease. Once the gastrointestinal mucosal tissues are penetrated by the larvae of nematodes, the interaction between epithelial cells, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), antigen-presenting cells (APC) such as dendritic cells and intestinal macrophages are stimulated to generate an immune response in co-regulation with complement fixation and mucus secretions to resist the primary infection (Garza 2014; McRae et al. 2015). Subsequently, to control the further secondary infections the specific adaptive immune mechanisms are triggered. The antigen specific immune mechanisms (processing and presentations) induce both humeral and cellular immunity. Th2 lymphocytes coordinate the humoral immune response which secrete the main cytokines IL3, IL4, IL5, IL9, IL10 and IL13 (Abo-Aziza et al. 2017; EL Namaky et al. 2017; Rodrigues et al. 2017). T-helper 2 cytokines drive the effector cell mechanisms which include eosinophils and mast cells. Additionally, the immunity against GINs is typically associated with different Ig isotypes (IgA, IgE and IgG) responses. IgA and IgE are the most characteristic features at the local mucosal sites of helminth infections, however IgG is predominantly detected in serum of infected animals (Angulo-Cubillán et al. 2007; McRae et al. 2015; Kandil et al. 2016). This host-parasite relationship is manifested by different phenomena as hypobiosis of larval stages, expulsion of adult stages, decreasing adult female fecundity, changes in morphological characters of the adult. Several factors could affect GINs parasitism and influence the immune responses developed against them. These factors could be a host factor; related to its genetic constitution, age and/or physiological status, management factors such as nutrition and chemoprophylaxis therapy or parasite factors which contributed to nematode immunomodulation strategy (Balic et al. 2000; González et al. 2003; McRae et al. 2015; González-Garduño et al. 2017). Hence, this review aimed to understand GINs-ruminants relationship and the effector immune strategies developed against them. This fundamental understanding highlights the right way to diagnose and control GINs infections in ruminants. Gastrointestinal nematodes of ruminants GINs are the major constraint to health, productivity and welfare of ruminants. Most species of these nematodes are related to order Strongylida, family Trichostrongyloidea. Most prevalent genera which infect small and large ruminants include Haemonchus, Cooperia, Ostertagia, Teladorsagia, Bunostomum, Trichostrongylus, Oesophagostomum, Chabertia, Nematodirus, Protostrongylus and Trichuris (Amarante and Amarante 2016; Belina et al. 2017). They usually habituate abomasum, small intestine and some lesser extent to large intestine. In general, the species of GINs are bounded to one host species. Nonetheless, particular exclusions are found among different ruminants such as Trichostrongylus axei (T. axei) and Haemonchus placei (H. placei) which is found in cattle and sheep. Haemonchus longistipes (H. longistipes) is a nematode of camel, but it can infect goats (Elshahawy et al. 2014). Published in final edited form as: Trends Parasitol. 2018 Aug 31;34(10):861–880. doi: 10.1016/j.pt.2018.08.007 Abstract Helminth infections represent a significant public health concern resulting in devastating morbidity and economic consequences across the globe. Helminths migrate through mucosal sites causing tissue damage and the induction of type 2 immune responses. Anti-helminth protection relies on the mobilization and activation of multiple immune cells including type 2 innate lymphocytes (ILC2s), basophils, mast cells, macrophages and hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells. Further, epithelial cells and neurons have been recognized as important regulators of type 2 immunity. Collectively, these pathways stimulate host-protective responses necessary for worm expulsion and the healing of affected tissues. In this review, we focus on the innate immune pathways that regulate immunity to helminth parasites and describe how better understanding these pathways may lead to the development of new therapeutic strategies. Keywords: Type 2 cytokines, innate immunity, mucosal immunology, helminth parasites Type 2 inflammation promotes host-protective responses to helminths Helminth infections constitute a serious public health concern affecting approximately one third of the global population, particularly in impoverished areas of Africa, Asia and South America[1, 2]. These high rates of infection are driven by a wide diversity of helminths that can cause human disease including but not limited to Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm), Trichuris trichiura, Trichinella spiralis (whipworms), Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus (hookworms), Strongyloides stercoralis as well as different Schistosoma and microfilariae species. Helminths often establish chronic infections resulting in anemia, malnutrition, growth impairment, cognitive deficiencies and immunopathology. Despite the implementation and effectiveness of anti-helminth medications, high reinfection rates are thought to limit their longterm impact. For example, recent studies have shown that approximately 50% of patients treated with anti-helminths will become reinfected within six months of receiving the medication[3]. In addition to humans, helminth infections are known to have devastating consequences on livestock populations. In order to combat this issue, many farmers have continuously administered anti-helminthic drugs resulting in the increased prevalence of drugresistant parasites[4]. Further, the generation of effective vaccines against helminths has been hindered due to the complexity of their life cycles, the antigenic variation of helminths at their distinct developmental stages and the multiple immunomodulatory mechanisms utilized by helminths to dampen host-protective responses[5]. Ruminant-specific features of trichostrongylid immunity are shaped by both broad immune principles and species-level variation. The evidence indicates that ruminants acquire protective, non-sterilizing immunity over time after exposure to gastrointestinal nematodes, and that this immunity is influenced by host genetics, nutrition, age, and physiological status [N4-R4]. That same source also notes that ruminant immunity is associated with Th2 cytokines and with IgA, IgE, and IgG responses, especially IgA and IgE at mucosal sites [N4-R1]. This suggests a species-specific immune profile centered on type 2 immunity and mucosal defenses rather than a single, uniform response.

On the ruminant-specific side, the evidence shows that trichostrongylid immunity is not species-blind. For example, the review notes that some trichostrongylid species are more prevalent in small ruminants, and that the immune response can vary across species because of antigen specificity and cross-species differences in protective immunity [N4-R2]. The same source also states that antigen(s) shared by related Trichostrongylus species may not be shared by N. spathiger, implying species-specific differences in immune recognition and protection [N4-R2]. This is an important clue for co-evolution: ruminants and their nematode parasites are engaged in an antigen-driven arms race, where parasite antigens can be conserved within related species but divergent across species, and host immunity must adapt to those differences [N4-R2].

Host-parasite co-evolution is further implied by the evidence that certain ruminant nematode species are effective at modulating mammalian host immunity [N4-R5]. This indicates that nematodes are not passive invaders; they actively shape host immune responses, which in turn may drive selection pressure on both sides. The evidence also suggests that immune evasion strategies are part of the host-parasite relationship, and that factors such as host genetics, age, and management influence parasitism and immune responses [N4-R1]. These co-evolutionary clues are consistent with the idea that ruminant immunity is both adaptive and context-dependent, rather than a fixed program.

The limitations and exceptions in ruminant immunity are also evident. The evidence emphasizes that immunity is non-sterilizing and that young, growing animals are especially vulnerable because they have not yet developed protective immunity [N4-R4]. This means immunity is often partial, and resistance is not absolute. The same source notes that immunity is affected by host, management, and parasite factors, so immunity cannot be predicted solely by one variable [N4-R1]. Additionally, the evidence implies that anthelmintic resistance and immune evasion by parasites can limit the effectiveness of host immunity [N4-R5]. These limitations show that ruminant immunity is practical but imperfect, and that immunity to trichostrongylids must be understood as a dynamic balance rather than a binary success/failure state [N4-R4][N4-R5].

The evidence for eosinophils and mast cells in larval rejection is strongest and most directly linked to trichostrongylid infection. The direct supporting evidence states that immune expulsion of the trichostrongylid Cooperia oncophora is associated with increased eosinophilia and mucosal IgA [N5-R2]. Another direct source reports that young lambs develop significant increases in inflammatory-cell-associated numbers in the intestine after infection with Nematodirus battus [N5-R5]. This aligns with the broader ruminant immunity review, which explicitly says that T-helper 2 cytokines drive effector cell mechanisms that include eosinophils and mast cells [N1-F1]. It also notes that immunity against gastrointestinal nematodes is typically associated with IgA, IgE, and IgG responses, with IgA and IgE being especially characteristic at mucosal sites [N1-F1].

The experimental evidence linking these cells to larval expulsion is therefore substantial. The direct evidence from the trichostrongylid study on Cooperia oncophora clearly links immune expulsion to increased eosinophilia and mucosal IgA [N5-R2]. The evidence from the lambs infected with Nematodirus battus shows increased inflammatory-cell infiltration in the intestine, consistent with a local immune response to larval presence [N5-R5]. In addition, the ruminant immunity review states that eosinophils preserve parasitic nematode larvae by regulating local immunity, which appears contradictory at first but may instead indicate that eosinophils are part of a broader immune regulation network that can both control and, under certain conditions, support larvae [N1-R1]. This suggests that the role of eosinophils is not purely destructive but may be more nuanced: they can participate in larval rejection while also influencing larval establishment or survival [N1-R1].

The evidence does not provide a simple parallel-versus-sequential distinction across all studies, but it does support a coordinated model. Eosinophils and mast cells are both described as effector cells driven by Th2 cytokines [N1-F1], and mast cells are specifically noted as being part of the innate immune pathways that regulate immunity to helminths [N2-F2]. That innate review also says that mast cells, along with eosinophils, basophils, ILC2s, and other cells, are mobilized and activated as part of the host-protective response to worms [N2-F2]. This suggests that the two cells likely act in parallel rather than strictly sequentially, because they are both part of the same early type 2 immune cascade. However, mast cells and eosinophils may also interact mechanistically: mast cells are activated early and can release mediators that influence the local environment, while eosinophils are later recruited and can directly damage larvae [N2-F2][N1-F1].

Function is measured in vivo and in vitro through several assays. In vivo, the evidence includes intestinal inflammatory-cell infiltration, increased eosinophilia, and mucosal IgA in infected lambs and sheep [N5-R5][N5-R2]. In the context of larval rejection, the evidence also mentions that challenge larvae mixed with immune mucus from sheep displaced larval migration when infused into naive recipients, suggesting a measurable rejection response in vivo [N3-R1]. For mast cells and eosinophils specifically, the innate review states that type 2 immune responses are characterized by the expansion and activation of innate immune cells including eosinophils, mast cells, ILC2s, and others, and that these responses are detected through cytokine secretion and immune-cell mobilization [N2-F2]. In the ruminant immunity review, the effector cell mechanisms are tied to Th2 cytokines and to IgA, IgE, and IgG responses, which are biomarkers of immune activation [N1-F1]. So, function is assessed by combining cell counts, cytokine profiles, Ig isotypes, and in vivo larval displacement assays [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R1].

Overall, the evidence strongly supports a role for eosinophils and mast cells in larval rejection, but that role is best understood as part of a coordinated type 2 immune response rather than as isolated, single-cell mechanisms [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence also supports in vivo measurement through larval displacement and inflammatory-cell infiltration, and in vitro measurement through immune-cell activation and cytokine assays [N3-R1][N5-R5][N2-F2].

The two overlapping immune mechanisms most consistently associated with larval rejection are the **type 2 innate immune response** and the **Th2-driven effector-cell response**. These mechanisms are tightly intertwined in the evidence provided.

The type 2 innate immune response is the first line of host defense. The innate review states that innate immune pathways regulate immunity to helminths and that the initial response belongs to the innate immune system, which senses parasites before the host can initiate an adaptive immune response [N2-R2][N2-R1]. That same review also says that helminth infections induce type 2 immune responses characterized by population expansion and activation of innate immune cells including dendritic cells, basophils, eosinophils, mast cells, ILC2s, and hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells [N2-F2]. In the ruminant immunity review, the innate response is described as a classical pathway that includes epithelial cells, ILCs, APCs such as dendritic cells and intestinal macrophages, complement fixation, and mucus secretions, all of which are activated when larvae penetrate the mucosa [N1-F1]. Taken together, these sources indicate that the innate response is not a passive bystander but an active, early, and multi-cellular barrier against larvae.

The Th2-driven effector-cell response is the second major mechanism. The ruminant immunity review explicitly states that T-helper 2 cytokines drive the effector cell mechanisms, including eosinophils and mast cells [N1-F1]. It also notes that immunity against gastrointestinal nematodes is associated with IgA, IgE, and IgG responses, with IgA and IgE being especially characteristic at mucosal sites [N1-F1]. The innate review similarly says that type 2 immunity promotes host-protective responses necessary for worm expulsion and tissue healing [N2-F2]. This shows that the Th2 response is not merely a downstream adaptive reaction; it is a central component of the immune strategy that mobilizes effector cells and cytokines to expel larvae.

Each mechanism contributes to larval clearance or expulsion in different ways. The innate response contributes by activating early innate immune cells and generating the initial signals that shape the adaptive response. The evidence suggests that epithelial cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, and ILCs are stimulated by larvae penetrating the mucosa, and that these cells regulate immune responses and produce mucus and other protective factors [N1-F1][N2-R2]. The Th2 effector-cell response contributes by recruiting and activating eosinophils, mast cells, and other effector cells, and by driving cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5, IL-9, and IL-13, which promote inflammation and expulsion [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The ruminant immunity review also states that immunity is associated with failure of larval establishment or hypobiosis, low worm burden, and decreased female fecundity [N1-F1]. This indicates that the mechanisms together reduce larval survival and reproduction rather than simply killing larvae outright.

Where the mechanisms overlap mechanistically, the evidence shows that they are deeply interdependent. Innate and adaptive pathways are described as co-regulated [N1-F1], and the innate review states that type 2 immunity is regulated by innate immune pathways and that epithelial cells and neurons are important regulators of type 2 immunity [N2-F2]. In this framework, the innate response primes the Th2 effector response, while the Th2 response amplifies and directs the innate response toward expulsion. The evidence also links mast cells and eosinophils to larval expulsion, showing that these effector cells are part of both the innate-like and Th2-driven arms of immunity [N5-R2][N5-R5][N1-F1]. The overlap is therefore not merely temporal; it is functional, with innate and Th2 pathways reinforcing each other to promote expulsion [N2-F2][N1-F1][N2-R2].

In summary, the two mechanisms are: 1) the innate type 2 immune response, which senses larvae and initiates protective inflammation; and 2) the Th2-driven effector-cell response, which recruits eosinophils, mast cells, and other cells to expel larvae and reduce parasite burden [N2-R2][N2-F2][N1-F1]. They overlap because the innate response sets the stage for Th2 effector activity, and the Th2 response strengthens and directs innate mechanisms toward expulsion [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## What are the two overlapping immune mechanisms by which ruminants reject incoming trichostrongylid larvae?

The two overlapping immune mechanisms most consistently associated with larval rejection in ruminants are the **type 2 innate immune response** and the **Th2-driven effector-cell response** [N2-R2][N2-R1][N2-F2][N1-F1]. These mechanisms are not separate pathways but deeply interconnected: the innate response primes and shapes the adaptive Th2 response, while the Th2 response amplifies and directs innate mechanisms toward expulsion [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### 1) Type 2 innate immune response
This is the first line of host defense against incoming trichostrongylid larvae. The evidence states that the innate immune system senses parasites before the host can initiate an adaptive immune response [N2-R2]. It also says that innate immune pathways regulate immunity to helminths and that type 2 immune responses are characterized by the expansion and activation of innate immune cells such as dendritic cells, basophils, eosinophils, mast cells, ILC2s, and hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells [N2-F2]. In the ruminant context, the innate response is described as a classical pathway that includes epithelial cells, ILCs, antigen-presenting cells (APCs) such as dendritic cells and intestinal macrophages, complement fixation, and mucus secretions, all activated when larvae penetrate the mucosa [N1-F1]. This means the innate response is not passive; it is active, multi-cellular, and early.

The contribution of this mechanism to larval clearance or expulsion is primarily through early inflammation and barrier defenses. It sets the stage for the later Th2 response by generating signals that shape immune activation and by producing mucus and other protective factors [N1-F1][N2-R2]. It also activates innate immune cells that later recruit and coordinate the effector response [N2-F2].

### 2) Th2-driven effector-cell response
This is the second major mechanism. The ruminant immunity review explicitly states that T-helper 2 cytokines drive the effector cell mechanisms, including eosinophils and mast cells [N1-F1]. The same source notes that immunity against gastrointestinal nematodes is associated with IgA, IgE, and IgG responses, especially IgA and IgE at mucosal sites [N1-F1]. The innate review similarly says that type 2 immunity promotes host-protective responses necessary for worm expulsion and tissue healing [N2-F2]. This shows that the Th2 response is central to the expulsion strategy, not merely a downstream adaptive reaction.

The contribution of this mechanism to larval clearance or expulsion is through recruitment and activation of effector cells, cytokine secretion, and mucosal inflammation. The evidence ties Th2 cytokines to IL-4, IL-5, IL-9, and IL-13, which promote inflammation and expulsion [N2-F2]. It also links Th2 responses to failure of larval establishment or hypobiosis, low worm burden, and decreased female fecundity [N1-F1]. In other words, the Th2 response reduces larval survival and reproduction rather than simply killing larvae outright [N1-F1].

### Where the mechanisms overlap or interact mechanistically
The overlap is functional and not merely chronological. The evidence shows that innate and adaptive pathways are co-regulated [N1-F1], and that innate immune pathways regulate type 2 immunity [N2-F2]. Epithelial cells and neurons are also described as important regulators of type 2 immunity [N2-F2]. In this framework, the innate response primes the Th2 effector response, while the Th2 response strengthens and directs innate mechanisms toward expulsion [N1-F1][N2-F2].

A practical example of this overlap is the role of eosinophils and mast cells. Both are part of the innate-like and Th2-driven arms of immunity [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The direct evidence on trichostrongylid Cooperia oncophora shows that immune expulsion is associated with increased eosinophilia and mucosal IgA [N5-R2]. The evidence on young lambs infected with Nematodirus battus also shows increased inflammatory-cell infiltration in the intestine [N5-R5]. This indicates that eosinophils and mast cells act in parallel rather than sequentially, because they are both mobilized by the same type 2 immune cascade [N2-F2][N1-F1].

The evidence indicates that ruminants acquire protective, non-sterilizing immunity over time after exposure to gastrointestinal nematodes, and that this immunity is influenced by host genetics, nutrition, age, and physiological status [N4-R4]. That same source also notes that ruminant immunity is associated with Th2 cytokines and with IgA, IgE, and IgG responses, especially IgA and IgE at mucosal sites [N4-R1]. This suggests a species-specific immune profile centered on type 2 immunity and mucosal defenses rather than a single, uniform response.

On the ruminant-specific side, the evidence shows that trichostrongylid immunity is not species-blind. For example, the review notes that some trichostrongylid species are more prevalent in small ruminants, and that the immune response can vary across species because of antigen specificity and cross-species differences in protective immunity [N4-R2]. The same source also states that antigen(s) shared by related Trichostrongylus species may not be shared by N. spathiger, implying species-specific differences in immune recognition and protection [N4-R2]. The evidence also suggests that immune evasion strategies are part of the host-parasite relationship, and that factors such as host genetics, age, and management influence parasitism and immune responses [N4-R1]. These co-evolutionary clues are consistent with the idea that ruminant immunity is both adaptive and context-dependent, rather than a fixed program.

The limitations and exceptions in ruminant immunity are also evident. The evidence emphasizes that immunity is non-sterilizing and that young, growing animals are especially vulnerable because they have not yet developed protective immunity [N4-R4]. This means immunity is often partial, and resistance is not absolute. The same source notes that immunity is affected by host, management, and parasite factors, so immunity cannot be predicted solely by one variable [N4-R1]. Additionally, the evidence implies that anthelmintic resistance and immune evasion by parasites can limit the effectiveness of host immunity [N4-R5].
